headline: High: shared filesystem and broad tool/network access create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks between Dify and open-webui.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can read/write uploaded knowledge base files and uses tools wired into agent/workflow apps; open-webui can access local/mounted files and MCP/OpenAPI tools. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's outputs from shared files or tools. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF both agents are connected to the same shared file or mounted volume, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF either agent parses the other's file or tool output as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate file/workspace mounts for the two agents.
Disable automatic instruction-following from retrieved documents.
Add provenance labels to shared artifacts.
Require human review before executing tool calls from imported content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dify touches knowledge base content, conversation logs, model provider API keys, and tool credentials; open-webui touches documents, notes, files, persistent memory, and API keys, with broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive data can flow from one agent into the other's outputs or third-party calls. The pairwise leakage path is credible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem, mounted volume, or synced workspace, sensitive files can be exposed across agents.
IF either agent is configured with the same API keys or tool credentials, secrets can be reused or exfiltrated through outbound calls.
mitigations: Use separate credentials per agent.
Remove shared mounts and sync folders.
Restrict outbound network destinations for both agents.
Store secrets only in per-agent secret managers.
Rotate any shared API keys immediately.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and write-capable file access surfaces; Dify can write the filesystem and run server-side code, while open-webui can access local/mounted files and spawn subprocesses. In a shared directory or shared mutable resource, concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The profiles do not show locking, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or mounted volume, file clobbering is possible.
IF both agents mutate shared app state without external locking, race conditions can corrupt outputs or configs.
mitigations: Assign disjoint write directories.
Add file locks around shared resources.
Run one agent read-only against shared artifacts.
Serialize writes through a single orchestrator.
Snapshot shared state before concurrent runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify is an orchestration platform with agent/workflow apps and tool wiring; open-webui supports plugins, tools, MCP, and function calling. That means one agent's output can become the other's input and then trigger downstream actions. Without a documented verification gate between them, erroneous or hallucinated content can cascade into real actions.
conditions: IF Dify feeds generated text into open-webui tools or workflows without verification, errors can propagate into actions.
IF open-webui forwards Dify-produced facts to external APIs or tools, hallucinations can become operational mistakes.
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents.
Require citations for any factual claims before tool execution.
Disable autonomous action tools on the receiving agent.
Log and review all cross-agent handoffs.
Use a human approval gate for external side effects.

E_compliance.rationale: Dify explicitly touches conversation logs and knowledge base content, while open-webui touches persistent memory, usage analytics, documents, and files. If the same regulated data class is routed through both, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not specify certifications or residency, so I keep this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is stored in both agents, retention and deletion obligations must be reconciled.
IF one deployment is subject to a stricter residency rule than the other, cross-flow can create a compliance mismatch.
mitigations: Map data classes to each agent.
Disable analytics on regulated data.
Set matching retention windows.
Document deletion/export procedures for both systems.
Keep regulated workloads in one agent only.
